---
title: "Struggle Against Apartheid"
subtitle: "From peaceful protest to armed resistance to Robben Island"
---

## Apartheid and the Defiance Campaign

When the National Party came to power in 1948, it formalized racial
segregation into the system known as apartheid. Mandela became a central
organizer of the ANC's 1952 Defiance Campaign, a mass civil disobedience
effort against unjust laws, which established him as a prominent national
figure — and led to his first serious clashes with the law, including a
suspended sentence and banning orders that restricted his movement and
associations.

## The Treason Trial

In 1956, Mandela and 155 other activists were arrested and charged with
treason for their political activities. The Treason Trial dragged on for
years before all defendants were acquitted in 1961, but it cemented
Mandela's role as a leading voice of the liberation movement and exposed him
to activists across the ideological spectrum.

## Sharpeville and the Turn to Armed Struggle

The 1960 Sharpeville Massacre, in which police killed 69 unarmed protesters,
was a turning point. The government banned the ANC, forcing the movement
underground. Concluding that non-violent protest alone could not overturn
apartheid, Mandela helped found **Umkhonto we Sizwe** ("Spear of the
Nation"), the armed wing of the ANC, in 1961, and became its first
commander-in-chief. The organization pursued a campaign of sabotage against
government and economic infrastructure while explicitly seeking to avoid
loss of life.

## Arrest and the Rivonia Trial

Mandela was arrested in 1962 and initially sentenced to five years for
incitement and leaving the country without a permit. In 1963, while already
imprisoned, he and several other ANC leaders were charged with sabotage and
conspiracy in what became known as the **Rivonia Trial**. Facing a possible
death sentence, Mandela used the dock as a platform, delivering his famous
"I Am Prepared to Die" speech from the dock in April 1964.

::: {.quote-block}
"I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all
persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities. It is an
ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an
ideal for which I am prepared to die."
:::

Mandela and several co-defendants were convicted and sentenced to life
imprisonment rather than death.

## Twenty-Seven Years in Prison

Mandela spent the first 18 years of his sentence on **Robben Island**,
performing hard labor in a lime quarry, before being transferred to Pollsmoor
Prison and later Victor Verster Prison. Despite the isolation, he continued
to study, mentor fellow prisoners, and — through smuggled communications and
clandestine negotiations — remained the symbolic center of the anti-apartheid
movement.

International pressure mounted throughout the 1980s: economic sanctions,
global divestment campaigns, and a worldwide "Free Mandela" movement kept his
name and cause visible even as he remained out of public view. By the late
1980s, secret talks had begun between Mandela and the apartheid government
about a negotiated transition.
